title: Application-scale fault-tolerant quantum computer

concept.text: A programmable quantum computer that protects its information well enough to complete a deep, useful computation beyond practical classical reach. It would encode information in logical qubits, distributing that information across physical qubits so that errors can be detected and corrected while computation proceeds. The intended breakthrough is an integrated machine with enough reliable logical qubits, logical operations and operating time for a specified application.

Error-corrected memory is an essential component, but an application machine must also perform reliable logical computation and coordinate its quantum processor with classical decoding and control. Decoding must process error information as fast as the processor generates it; this throughput requirement does not mean that every correction requires feedback within the same error-correction cycle. Successful operation must account for both sustained throughput and the response latency required by the chosen algorithm and architecture.

significance.text: Such a machine would make known quantum algorithms executable at consequential scales. Shor’s factoring algorithm supplies a concrete basis for attacking RSA, whose security depends on the practical difficulty of factoring large integers. The missing capability is a sufficiently reliable implementation at the required scale. A successful attack on an appropriate 2048-bit RSA instance would have direct cryptographic significance, but it would not establish the ability to break every public-key system or execute every cryptanalytic workload.

Quantum simulation and quantum chemistry offer another basis for revolutionary impact: suitable quantum algorithms could calculate properties of matter at sizes and accuracies beyond practical classical methods. Each useful result would still require an executable algorithm, adequate hardware resources and a defensible comparison with the best applicable classical methods. The supplied evidence supports this conditional opportunity; it does not establish a general classical complexity lower bound or an advantage for every chemistry problem.

Synthesis: the advance would introduce a new practical computing capability for suitable problems, rather than merely increase classical processing speed. Routine industrial chemistry, materials discovery and changes to deployed cryptographic infrastructure would remain conditional downstream outcomes requiring further scientific, algorithmic and deployment work. Demonstrating one application would establish that capability at its demonstrated scale, not all possible applications.

Verified sampling is a meaningful computational achievement, but it does not by itself provide factoring or useful matter simulation. The supplied sampling preprint addresses trusted execution of error-detected sampling circuits and their hardness guarantees. Its workload and fidelity evidence must be assessed on those terms rather than treated as evidence that an application-scale fault-tolerant machine already exists.

missing_breakthrough.text: The unsolved capability illustrated by the supplied work is sustained, reliable logical computation at the qubit count and circuit depth required by a demanding application. Physical qubits lose coherence and experience operational errors. Below-threshold error correction makes larger codes improve logical reliability, but a successful memory experiment does not establish that sufficiently many logical qubits can interact and compute within a complete application error budget.

Concrete engineering barriers include physical-qubit overhead, reliable logical interactions, correlated error bursts, decoder scaling, and the calibration, compilation and control of a much larger processor. Rare correlated failures matter because they can undermine reliability extrapolations based on ordinary local errors. Connectivity constrains the architecture and the cost of moving or interacting encoded information; the supplied evidence does not establish it as an independent universal blocker for every architecture.

Error detection with post-selection cannot indefinitely substitute for scalable correction. Rejecting runs when detected errors occur can improve the retained output, but the acceptance rate falls as the computation grows. An application machine must deliver reliable results at a practical total cost, accounting for rejected runs, decoding, control and the resources consumed throughout execution.

current_state.text: Google Quantum AI and collaborators demonstrated below-threshold surface-code quantum memory in work published online on 9 December 2024 and appearing in Nature 638, 920–926 in 2025. The supplied research reports a 101-qubit distance-7 code with logical error of 0.143% ± 0.003% per cycle, error suppression Λ = 2.14 ± 0.02, and a logical lifetime 2.4 ± 0.3 times that of the best physical qubit. These measurements characterize a logical memory, not execution of a large factoring or chemistry algorithm.

The same research reports correlated events in repetition-code experiments at roughly one per hour, illustrating a rare-error mechanism relevant to scaling rather than a universal failure rate for quantum computers. It also records an author correction dated 28 April 2026, but the supplied review does not describe that correction’s contents or establish whether it changes any quoted metric. The review relied on explicit prose in the fully extracted main paper; figures were not visually inspected, and availability of supplementary files does not establish that all supplementary evidence was reviewed.

Martiel and colleagues’ preprint, Sampling hard circuits with verifiably high fidelity, has a supplied version-3 date of 2 September 2026. The validated review identifies an experiment with 64 data qubits and 76 physical qubits, using error detection, syndrome post-selection and a device-dependent fidelity bound. This corrects the earlier research’s 70-qubit/97-physical-qubit description. The preprint explicitly recognizes that post-selection overhead prevents error detection alone from scaling indefinitely. The supplied research did not identify a peer-reviewed version; the record does not independently establish its publication status at the cutoff.

Additional sampling figures in the earlier research—depth 70, 468 T gates, a 95% confidence fidelity lower bound of 0.284, and approximately 2,000 samples in 16 minutes—remain unresolved in this record. The validated review does not reconcile those quantities with its corrected experimental configuration, so they cannot safely be combined into one confirmed description. The retained PDF extraction is truncated in later supplementary material, although the review found sufficient explicit text to establish the limited claims about error-detected sampling and its scaling constraint. That limitation does not show that the earlier numerical assertions are false.

Craig Gidney’s resource-estimation preprint projects factoring a 2048-bit RSA integer in less than a week using fewer than one million noisy qubits. It assumes a square nearest-neighbor grid, uniform 0.1% depolarizing gate noise, a 1 µs surface-code cycle and a 10 µs control reaction time, together with further algorithmic and architectural assumptions. The reviewed artifact identifies a May 2025 submission and June 2025 manuscript date, correcting the earlier research’s August 2026 dating. This is a projected resource cost, not a device or completed factoring computation; detailed cold-storage workload analysis was left to future work. Extraction warnings limited the review, but did not obscure the passages supporting these assumptions and estimates.

Taken together, these sources document a gap between a roughly hundred-physical-qubit memory or sampling demonstration and an application architecture projected to require far greater resources and sustained reliability. They do not define a universal million-qubit requirement: resource needs depend on the application, code, hardware and algorithm. Neither supplied experiment meets the proposed application-scale criterion. Because no bounded freshness search was supplied, this record cannot establish whether other work had met that criterion by 1 November 2026.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed criterion, not an established standard: complete a specified application instance beyond practical classical reach, with a stated validation method and a complete error budget. One illustrative target is factoring a nontrivial 2048-bit RSA integer without prior access to its factors. Gidney’s estimate makes that target quantitatively concrete under its assumptions, but neither one million qubits nor one week is a universal completion threshold.
completion_criteria.label: Application beyond practical classical reach with validation and error budget

completion_criteria.text: Proposed alternative: solve a specified electronic-structure problem at a size and accuracy beyond the best applicable classical methods. A convincing demonstration would identify the physical system, requested observable, accuracy target, classical comparator and method for validating the result. Difficulty of classical simulation alone would not establish scientific usefulness, and a generic claim of quantum chemistry advantage would be insufficient.
completion_criteria.label: Fully specified electronic-structure problem beyond best applicable classical methods

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility requirements: disclose the workload, encoding, logical operations, physical and logical error measurements, decoding and control performance, runtime, total resource use and any rejected runs. Repeat the computation sufficiently to quantify success probability and uncertainty, with independent reproduction where feasible. Evidence of error suppression across code sizes should be accompanied by evidence that logical operations remain reliable during the actual computation, rather than inferred solely from a memory experiment.
completion_criteria.label: Full disclosure, quantified success, and logical reliability during computation

completion_criteria.text: Proposed practical boundary: assess the entire execution, including post-selection losses and classical support, against the claimed application outcome. A few thousand post-selected gates on roughly a hundred physical qubits would not by themselves satisfy this criterion. A successful finite set of demonstrations would establish the machine’s tested breadth and operating conditions; it would not prove literal universality across all workloads, noise conditions or scales.
completion_criteria.label: Entire execution including post-selection meets claimed outcome within tested conditions

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: CPE-02, Room-temperature general-purpose adiabatic reversible computer, shares concerns about computation and physical resource cost, but targets reversible classical computation and energy dissipation. CPE-01 targets reliable quantum computation using encoded quantum information. Reversibility alone does not establish the quantum capabilities described here.

Roster-based synthesis: CPE-03, General-purpose fabric that retires data-movement dominance, overlaps through the importance of communication and control architecture, but addresses the cost of moving data in general-purpose computing. CPE-04, Cascadable general-purpose photonic computer with optical memory, concerns an optical computing substrate and memory. Neither title by itself specifies quantum error correction or application-scale logical quantum computation; photonic implementation and fault-tolerant quantum capability are distinct properties.

Roster-based synthesis: CPE-05, Mammalian-scale neuromorphic learning machine near biological energy, targets learning capability and energy efficiency inspired by nervous systems, rather than execution of quantum algorithms. CPE-06, Wall-plug-superior superconducting classical computer at useful scale, may share cryogenic engineering concerns with some quantum architectures, but explicitly targets classical computation and total energy advantage. Superconducting hardware alone does not make a computer quantum.

Roster-based synthesis: CPE-07, Utility-scale quantum-repeater internet, overlaps most directly through the preservation and management of quantum information. Its central capability is quantum communication over a network; CPE-01 concerns sustained logical computation. A repeater network does not by itself demonstrate an application-scale quantum processor, and this record does not make a utility-scale network a prerequisite for such a processor.

Roster-based synthesis: CPE-08, Economically manufacturable atomic-density defect-tolerant digital computer, shares the challenge of building useful computation from imperfect physical components. Its title concerns manufacturing density and defect-tolerant digital computing, whereas CPE-01 requires protection of quantum information during operation. These entries remain separate. Their relationships are inferred from the supplied titles; detailed specifications and the separate ten historical entries were not supplied.

brief.title: A quantum computer that can finish useful calculations
possible: Researchers could calculate properties of molecules and materials beyond the practical reach of conventional computers. A programmable quantum computer would protect its information against errors long enough to finish a demanding, useful calculation.
Such a machine could also find the factors of large numbers used in RSA, an encryption system whose security depends on that task being impractical.
why: For scientists studying matter, this would open a way to answer questions that conventional computing cannot practically resolve. It would add a distinct computing capability for suitable problems.
For people responsible for secure communications, successful factoring would demonstrate a practical attack on RSA and give concrete meaning to the need for replacement encryption.

sources.showed: They demonstrated quantum memory whose protection improved as they added qubits, the physical units holding quantum information. The protected information also lasted longer than in the best individual qubit.
sources.quote: In this work, we realize surface codes operating below the threshold on two Willow processors.
sources.cited_for: Error correction can improve quantum memory as its protective encoding grows.
sources.not_established: The experiment did not demonstrate a demanding application with reliable operations throughout the computation.

sources.showed: In a preprint, Gidney estimated a lower hardware requirement for attacking RSA, using changes to the algorithm and the way information is protected and stored.
sources.quote:
Inthispaper, Isubstantially
reduce the number of qubits required.
sources.cited_for: A resource estimate connects the factoring target to a proposed machine design.
sources.not_established: The estimate assumes hardware performance and architectural choices that have not been demonstrated together in a working application.

sources.showed: In a preprint, they demonstrated sampling, drawing outputs from a quantum calculation, with error detection and a bound on output accuracy. They compared syndromes, signals that flag errors, before and after changing the calculation.
sources.quote:
We experimentally confirm that
the syndrome distributions remain nearly identical.
sources.cited_for: Error detection can accompany a demanding sampling calculation with a measurable bound on accuracy.
sources.not_established: Discarding runs with detected errors cannot scale indefinitely, and sampling does not demonstrate useful factoring or matter simulation.

shown: Google Quantum AI and collaborators demonstrated protected quantum memory that became more reliable as its encoding grew. This establishes a necessary building block: logical qubits, which spread information across physical qubits to protect it.
Martiel and collaborators demonstrated error-detected sampling with a bound on accuracy. Neither experiment completed a demanding factoring or chemistry application with sustained error correction.
missing: Enough logical qubits must interact reliably throughout a demanding application.
Classical computers must interpret error signals and control the processor fast enough throughout the calculation.
A larger machine must control rare bursts of correlated errors that can defeat ordinary reliability estimates.
A complete application must succeed at a practical total cost, including discarded runs and classical support.

milestones.label: A validated application beyond conventional computing
milestones.explanation: A specified application would have to finish beyond practical conventional reach, with a validation method and an accounting of all error sources. This would establish useful computation at the demonstrated scale.

milestones.label: A validated calculation of electrons beyond conventional methods
milestones.explanation: An alternative demonstration would solve a specified problem about electrons in matter beyond the best applicable conventional methods, at a stated accuracy with validation. This would establish the chemistry route.

milestones.label: Repeated success with reliable logical operations
milestones.explanation: Repeated runs and full disclosure would have to quantify success, errors, resources and control performance, with independent reproduction where feasible. This would establish reliability during computation.

milestones.label: The complete execution meets the application claim
milestones.explanation: The full execution would have to deliver the claimed result while counting discarded runs and classical support. This would establish practical success within the machine’s tested operating conditions.

uncertain: The hardware needed depends on the application, error protection and algorithm; the factoring estimate is conditional.
The chemistry target still needs a specific physical system, accuracy requirement, conventional comparison and validation method.
The origins of rare correlated errors, and their effect on much larger machines, remain open.

page.title: Utility-scale fault-tolerant quantum computer
page.definition: A programmable quantum computer executes applications with computational value exceeding its acquisition, operation and maintenance costs. Repeated quantum error correction protects logical qubits, which distribute quantum information across physical components, throughout computation.

goal.need: Factoring a 2048-bit RSA integer would compromise that RSA key. Gidney’s preprint of 21 May 2025 estimates fewer than one million noisy qubits and less than one week for this workload, assuming uniform 0.1% gate errors, 1 μs surface-code cycles and 10 μs control reaction time on a square nearest-neighbour grid. These are conditional resource estimates, not a completed factorization.

statements.quote: achieve utility-scale operation — meaning its computational value exceeds its cost.

statements.body: US Department of Energy, Quantum Genesis Q Competition
statements.quote: a fault-tolerant quantum computer of sufficient performance to qualify as “scientifically relevant.”
the destination is utility-scale quantum computing, which involves computations that deliver clear practical value on real workloads.

completion.title: An operating fault-tolerant quantum computer delivers computational value exceeding its lifetime cost.
completion.criterion: Operate a programmable, fault-tolerant quantum computer whose computational value exceeds its customer’s acquisition, operation and maintenance costs over a reasonable system lifetime. DARPA’s cost boundary does not require recovery of all preceding R&D costs. Include repeated quantum error correction during execution and the costs of classical decoding, feedback and repeated runs. DARPA specifies no universal qubit count, gate count, runtime or output-error cutoff.
completion.set_by: DARPA, Quantum Benchmarking Initiative solicitation DARPA-PS-24-26, Section II.B.3 and footnote 4.
completion.threshold_quote: DARPA qualitatively defines a utility-scale quantum computer as a system whose computational value exceeds its costs.
completion.basis: This adopts DARPA’s system-level definition and customer-cost boundary. Microsoft and Qolab identify repeated error correction, universal logical operations and real-time control as requirements for the underlying capability. QBI Stage C assesses readiness to construct a machine; passing it does not demonstrate utility-scale operation.

milestones.title: A quantum memory suppresses errors as its encoding grows while its decoder keeps pace with measurements.
milestones.criterion: Demonstrate logical error suppression as the encoding grows while decoding measurements at least as fast as they arrive. Google’s paper of 9 December 2024 reports a real-time distance-5 surface-code memory over up to 1,000,000 correction cycles (1.1 μs per cycle; 63 μs mean decoding latency). A separate 101-physical-qubit distance-7 memory had 0.143% ± 0.003% error per cycle and suppression factor 2.14 ± 0.02 per distance increase of two (100,000 repetitions per memory-duration point). The correction of 28 April 2026 changes Figure 3a’s repetition-code labels.
milestones.set_by: Field conventions for below-threshold correction and streaming decoding, applied by Google Quantum AI in Nature; the demonstrated implementation uses superconducting surface codes.
milestones.threshold_quote: the syndrome information produced by the quantum device must be decoded as fast as it is generated

milestones.title: A quantum processor implements a universal set of fault-tolerant logical gates.
milestones.criterion: Implement encoded gates forming a universal set, sufficient to approximate arbitrary quantum computations, with fault-tolerant circuit designs and better performance than corresponding non-fault-tolerant designs. Postler et al. demonstrated this on two logical qubits, each encoded in seven trapped ions, on 25 May 2022. Martiel et al.’s preprint revised on 2 September 2026 reports 64 data qubits encoded using 76 physical qubits with error detection and post-selection; this tests a different capability from sustained error correction.
milestones.set_by: Fault-tolerant universal-gate convention, applied by Postler et al. in Nature; their experimental test used trapped ions.
milestones.threshold_quote: We observe the hallmark feature of fault tolerance—a superior performance compared with a non-fault-tolerant implementation.

milestones.title: A prototype runs a scientific subroutine with about 10 logical qubits and 1,000 hard operations.
milestones.criterion: DOE’s illustrative prototype target is 10 logical qubits, 1,000 reliably completed hard operations and a scientific subroutine. Hard operations are code-dependent operations needed for universality, such as non-Clifford gates. Acceptance metrics are negotiated.
milestones.set_by: DOE, DE-FOA-0003657, Table 1 (illustrative numerical target tabulated).

milestones.title: A quantum computer runs a scientific workflow with about 100 logical qubits and 100,000 hard operations.
milestones.criterion: DOE’s illustrative first-generation target is 100 logical qubits, 100,000 hard operations and a complete scientific workflow. The workflow need not be classically intractable; architecture-specific acceptance metrics are negotiated.
milestones.set_by: DOE, DE-FOA-0003657, Table 1 (illustrative numerical target tabulated).

milestones.title: A quantum computer performs discovery science with about 1,000 logical qubits and 10 million hard operations.
milestones.criterion: DOE’s illustrative next-generation target is 1,000 logical qubits, 10 million hard operations and production-level discovery science. This stage lies beyond the Q Competition’s funded final milestone.
milestones.set_by: DOE, DE-FOA-0003657, Table 1 (illustrative numerical target tabulated).

not_found: No public, architecture-independent numerical method for establishing computational value exceeding cost was found in QBI’s programme material or solicitation.
Searches for demonstrated utility-scale fault-tolerant operation and production-level quantum discovery science did not establish completion for any listed hardware platform as of 14 November 2026.
No peer-reviewed version of Martiel et al.’s sampling preprint was identified.

results.finding: A surface-code memory on a 72-qubit processor maintained below-threshold performance with real-time decoding for up to 1 million cycles.
results.detail: The distance-5 real-time decoder had 63 μs mean latency and a suppression factor of 2.0 ± 0.1 per distance increase of two. A separate 101-qubit distance-7 memory was decoded offline.
results.quote: Our system maintains below-threshold performance when decoding in real time, achieving an average decoder latency of 63 microseconds at distance 5 up to a million cycles, with a cycle time of 1.1 microseconds.

results.finding: A 64-data-qubit encoded circuit suppressed effective gate errors 10× after post-selection.
results.detail: The experiment used error detection and post-selection. It did not demonstrate a universal set of fault-tolerant logical gates.
results.quote:
We use a total of 76 physical qubits to encode this computation in
spacetime codes, effectively suppressing gate error rates by 10×after syndrome post-selection

results.finding: A 64-qubit encoded sampling circuit included 314 T gates.
results.detail: The experiment did not run a scientific subroutine or demonstrate 1,000 reliably completed fault-tolerant hard operations; it used error detection and post-selection.
results.quote:
We demonstrate our proposal with a 64-qubit, depth-73 Clifford
circuit, doped with 314Tgates.

results.finding: Trapped-ion memory: 66,440 shots across distances 3, 5 and 7; logical errors fell by a factor of 12 +3−2 per distance increase of two.
results.detail: All decoding was performed offline. Streaming decoders processed recorded measurements one round at a time; their timing was measured separately, without end-to-end real-time feedback latency.
results.quote:
Leveraging both circuit- and hardware-
level leakage reduction schemes, we achieve logical error rates as low as 5+4−2 ×10 −6, and demonstrate
error suppression by over an order of magnitude, Λ = 12 +3−2, with each successive increase in code
distance.

results.finding: Neutral-atom toric memory: approximately 39,000 and 23,500 shots per point; average error suppression factor 1.30 ± 0.03 at four cycles.
results.detail: The larger code showed lower logical error rates at 4, 6 and 8 cycles without reservoir reloading. The text reports decoding recorded bitstrings but does not demonstrate that decoding kept pace with measurements.
results.quote:
Averaging over the two
observables, we observe ΛAvgno reload = 1.30±.03.

results.finding: A trapped-ion processor demonstrated a fault-tolerant universal gate set on two logical qubits.
results.detail: Each logical qubit used a seven-qubit colour code. The authors report superior performance compared with a non-fault-tolerant implementation.
results.quote: Here we demonstrate a fault-tolerant universal set of gates on two logical qubits in a trapped-ion quantum computer.

results.finding: Trapped-ion processor implemented a fault-tolerant universal gate set on 3 logical qubits encoded in 8 physical qubits.
results.detail: The gates use an error-detecting code and post-selection. The text does not establish better performance of the universal gate set than corresponding non-fault-tolerant designs; its comparison concerns logical teleportation.
results.quote: Moreover, we realize a fault-tolerant universal gate set on an eight-qubit error-detecting code hosting three logical qubits, based on state injection, which can be executed by coherent gate operations only.

results.finding: Neutral-atom processor synthesized rotations on logical qubits encoded in 15-atom blocks using up to 3 T gates.
results.detail: The experiment used transversal teleportation for universal logic, with feedforward applied in software. The text does not establish better gate performance than corresponding non-fault-tolerant designs.

results.finding: Two superconducting logical qubits demonstrated a non-Clifford logical rotation with 0.943 post-selected gate fidelity.
results.detail: The magic-state initialization was non-fault-tolerant, and the gate-teleportation implementation was not fully fault-tolerant. The source does not demonstrate a universal fault-tolerant gate set with better performance than corresponding non-fault-tolerant designs.
results.quote:

results.finding: IBM superconducting processor: Ising-model simulations used 42 logical qubits.
results.detail: The simulations used error detection and postselection with non-fault-tolerant logical operations. The source does not establish 1,000 reliably completed hard operations or repeated error correction throughout the computation.
results.quote: By retaining all intra-block connections and removing specific inter-block edges from the grid, we implement a chain of 42 logical qubits

results.detail: The QFT is a foundational subroutine, but the report does not establish 1,000 reliably completed hard operations or repeated error correction throughout the computation. The 12-qubit acceptance rate reflects error-detection post-selection.
